title: Why a written code
hook: a shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike

segments.voice: Yesterday, the old rehatnamas: earlier codes that share much and differ in detail. Your line was codes change, the guru doesn't. Which rule did you question, and what was it protecting? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.

A woman lands in a city she has never seen, tired, a long way from her family. She finds a gurdwara on a side street. She doesn't know a single person inside. But at the door she already knows what to do. Shoes off. Head covered. Into the hall, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, sit with the sangat. Later, down to the langar, where she sits on the floor in a row with strangers and is fed. Nobody had to explain any of it. Countless small things were already shared before she arrived. Today asks how that happens, and why Sikhs bothered to write it down.
screen: `A STRANGER IN A NEW CITY.` → `SHE ALREADY KNOWS WHAT TO DO.` → `WHY WRITE IT DOWN?`

segments.voice: Take four reasons, one at a time. First, a written code travels. Spoken custom stays close to the village it grew in. A page can be carried across an ocean, read in a new language, taught in a basement class in a city the Gurus never saw. So a Sikh family in one country and a Sikh family in another can open the same pages and find the same daily prayers, the same order for a wedding, the same form for the Ardas. One code, many homes. Second, a written code settles things more fairly. When two people disagree about how something should be done, they can point to a page instead of to whoever speaks loudest or has the most money. A rule on paper applies to the powerful as well as the poor. Third, it gives a starting place to the newcomer. Someone learning the path, or coming back to it after years away, can read what is asked instead of guessing or feeling foolish. And fourth, it keeps the community in conversation. The shared code was agreed by Sikhs working together, and the Guru Panth can still discuss it. A written code doesn't replace the Guru. It doesn't replace love, or seva, or the remembrance of the Name. It is more like a common doorway. Different families still bring their own warmth, their own food, their own way of laughing in the langar line. But the doorway is the same width wherever you find it, and anyone can walk through.
screen: `A PAGE CAN CROSS AN OCEAN.` · `POINT TO A PAGE, NOT A VOICE.` · `A STARTING PLACE FOR NEWCOMERS.` · `A COMMON DOORWAY, NOT THE GURU.` · then, large: `ONE CODE, MANY HOMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one family rule. Settle, and breathe. Your family, or your household, already has rules nobody wrote down. Who takes off shoes at the door. Who sits where. What gets said before a meal. Choose one that matters to you. Now put it into one plain sentence, the way it would read on a page for someone who just moved in. Jot it on anything nearby, or shape the words silently. Then sit with it until the bell. Does the sentence say everything the habit does, or did something get lost on the way to the page? The bell holds the time.
Why a written code. A shared code lets Sikhs everywhere practice alike: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Today's word.
Your line: one code, many homes. Today, show someone new how something is done where you live or work, plainly, so they don't have to guess. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-six.
